---
title: "Authorship, collaboration and corrections"
last-reviewed: "2026-09-06"
---

You're preparing a paper and someone asks who will be listed as an author. The team remembers the original plan differently, and the person who ended up doing the analysis wasn't on it. This is an awkward time to reconstruct everyone's contribution.

Talk about credit when you agree the work, then revisit it as roles change. We'll separate authorship from acknowledgement and ownership, work through a changed contribution, and cover how to correct a record when something is wrong.

## Discuss credit early {#agree-credit-while-the-work-can-still-be-redesigned}

Discuss contributions before substantial work begins, record provisional expectations, revisit them when work changes, and apply the authorship standard governing the output. Authorship is not a reward for status, access, supervision, funding or goodwill alone.

If an error affects evidence, attribution, participant or community interests, confidentiality or decisions, preserve the records and seek advice promptly. The correction process is covered later in this chapter.

## Separate contribution, authorship, acknowledgement and ownership

These are different decisions:

- **Contribution** describes work performed.
- **Authorship** assigns public credit and accountability under a governing standard.
- **Acknowledgement** recognises contributions that do not meet authorship criteria, usually with permission where naming implies endorsement.
- **Ownership and intellectual property** concern legal or contractual rights in data, materials, inventions, copyright or knowledge.
- **Access and custody** concern who can hold, use, transfer or preserve records.

A person may own data without qualifying as an author. A person may qualify for authorship without owning the output. A community may hold governance authority that cannot be reduced to an individual contributor role.

The Australian Code requires authors to have made a significant intellectual or scholarly contribution and agree to be listed, and requires appropriate acknowledgement of contributions [@australian-code-2018]. Apply the current local and venue-specific interpretation rather than treating this summary as a universal threshold.

## Use contribution roles without turning them into an authorship calculator

CRediT provides 14 standard roles for describing contributions, such as conceptualisation, methodology, investigation, data curation, software, visualisation, supervision and writing [@credit-taxonomy]. It improves specificity, but it does not decide who qualifies as an author or what order authors should appear.

For each planned output, record:

- work already completed;
- work still expected;
- evidence of the contribution;
- responsibility for checking relevant content;
- provisional authorship status and order;
- the governing standard; and
- the next review trigger.

Use future contributions as expectations, not facts. “Will lead analysis” cannot justify final authorship if the work never occurs.

## Hold the conversation at decision points

At minimum, revisit authorship and contributions:

1. when an output is first proposed;
2. when roles are allocated;
3. after a material method, staffing or scope change;
4. before a full draft is circulated;
5. before submission;
6. after major revision; and
7. before any correction, retraction or derivative output.

Changes are normal. Secret or status-driven changes are not.

### A useful meeting sequence

- Identify the exact output—not “the project” in general.
- Read the applicable authorship and contribution standard.
- Review actual and expected work person by person.
- Discuss accountability and who can verify each part.
- Propose order using the disciplinary convention and explain it.
- Identify conflicts, missing work and dependencies.
- Record provisional agreement and what would trigger change.
- Confirm the record with everyone, including dissent or unresolved issues.

## Example: expected analysis does not happen

**Initial record:** Candidate A will lead conceptualisation, data collection, analysis and drafting; Statistician B will advise on design and verify analysis; Supervisor C will contribute to methodology and substantive revision. Provisional order: A, B, C, subject to completed contributions.

**What changes:** B leaves the project before analysis. Statistician D reconstructs the model, identifies a serious error, performs the analysis and drafts the technical methods. B provided one early consultation but does not review or approve the manuscript.

**Bad response:** retain the original order because it was “promised”, or remove B privately without discussion.

**Defensible response:** update the contribution record; apply the governing authorship criteria to completed work; invite B to clarify and, if appropriate, complete remaining author responsibilities; assess D's actual intellectual contribution and accountability; discuss revised order with all proposed authors; retain the decision and dissent; acknowledge non-author contributions appropriately.

The initial conversation created expectations, not permanent entitlement.

## Design collaboration before conflict

For academic, industry, government, service, community or international collaboration, agree early on:

- purpose, values and decision rights;
- roles, authority and escalation;
- data, materials, knowledge and intellectual-property governance;
- Indigenous and community protocols where relevant;
- confidentiality and public communication;
- publication review and reasonable timeframes;
- conflicts of interest;
- funding and resource commitments;
- authorship and acknowledgement standards;
- record locations, access and handover;
- changes, withdrawal and project closure; and
- what happens when agreements conflict.

Do not promise a partner control that the university, ethics approval, law or research-integrity standard does not permit. Do not describe consultation as co-design or partnership when affected people had no decision power.

## Recognise power and protect disagreement

Students may fear that questioning authorship, data use or reporting will affect supervision, references, employment or examination. Build a pathway that does not require confronting the most powerful person first.

Possible routes include:

- a documented clarification conversation where safe;
- an independent supervisor or graduate research coordinator;
- a research integrity adviser;
- an authorship, dispute or complaints process;
- an ethics, governance, data or community authority; and
- confidential student or staff support.

Check the local process and confidentiality limits. Distinguish seeking advice from making a formal allegation.

## Correct the record

When a possible error is found:

1. preserve the source data, files, communications, versions and outputs;
2. state what is known, suspected and unknown;
3. assess immediate welfare, privacy, legal, cultural and decision consequences;
4. stop affected analysis, recruitment, release or reuse where necessary;
5. notify the appropriate responsible people or bodies;
6. reproduce the issue and determine its scope;
7. correct the process and verify the correction;
8. assess whether prior conclusions, participants, collaborators, funders or readers are affected;
9. use the venue's correction, withdrawal, retraction or update mechanism; and
10. retain a transparent record without unnecessary personal accusation.

Australian publication guidance recommends accurate citation of primary sources where appropriate, transparency and timely correction of the record [@nhmrc-publication-guide]. The exact route depends on whether the material is an internal report, thesis, preprint, repository release, grant report or published article.

### Distinguish mistakes from misconduct

Do not diagnose intent from a discrepancy. Honest error, poor practice, dispute and potential breach require different evidence and processes. Protect records, use neutral factual language and seek the authorised process.

## Difficult disclosures

A disclosure should identify:

- what happened or changed;
- which version, output, people or decisions may be affected;
- immediate controls already taken;
- what remains uncertain;
- who has authority to decide the next step; and
- what evidence will confirm correction.

Avoid both minimisation (“just a minor issue”) and unsupported accusation. If participant safety, confidentiality, illegal conduct or immediate harm is possible, use the urgent local route.

## How vague roles become authorship conflict

Revisit credit when the work changes, using completed contributions and the applicable criteria. Supervision, funding, editing and data ownership don't automatically establish authorship. CRediT describes roles; it doesn't award points towards an author position.

Describe partnerships according to the decision power people had, and check contracts against research-integrity obligations. When correcting an error, preserve the originals and seek confidential advice promptly, even while its full extent is uncertain.

## When the contribution record is ready for the next stage

Use the checklist below with the current contribution record. Resolve acknowledgement and permission to name non-authors too. Any unresolved disagreement should stay visible as the output moves to its next stage.

## Bring the contribution record into the conversation

Bring the current output, applicable authorship standard and [contribution record](../../templates/authorship-conversation.qmd). Separate completed work from outstanding commitments, explain the proposed decision and identify any contractual, data, ethics or community constraints. Say whether you need agreement, independent advice or a formal process.

## Revisit credit at every major handover

- [ ] Contribution, authorship, acknowledgement, ownership and access are separated.
- [ ] The governing standard is current and identified.
- [ ] Completed and expected work are not confused.
- [ ] Author order has a stated disciplinary rationale.
- [ ] All proposed authors can review, approve and accept accountability as required.
- [ ] Community, cultural, partner, data and IP rights are respected.
- [ ] Conflicts and power-sensitive escalation routes are known.
- [ ] Errors preserve original records and trigger proportionate review.
- [ ] Corrections reach every affected version and audience.
- [ ] The contribution and correction records have review dates.
